"A Yalta format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the end of a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin just hours after Trump, Putin and Xi held talks in China.

European leaders have forcefully rejected any attempts to re-enact the 1945 Yalta Conference to end Russia's war on Ukraine and split the continent into spheres of influence.

The pushback went public on Thursday at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, comprising Kyiv's allies, hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The gathering in Berlin took place just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, dubbed "Yalta 2.0" by media commentators.

Trump, Putin and Xi discussed Ukraine, but their joint statement, titled "Declaration Toward Peace", did not mention the country.

"A Yalta format will not bring peace," Merz said, flanked by other leaders.

"At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again."

Merz gifted the over 40 delegations that took part in the talks a piece of the Berlin Wall, which, he said, is "what Yalta represented".

By his side, French President Emmanuel Macron said the four-point statement issued by Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen did not replicate the outcome of the 1945 conference, which set the stage for the four-decade-long Cold War.

"I don't think that it amounts to a reorganisation of the world," he said.

"If there is one critical element for the reorganisation of Europe and its security, it is the meeting that took place (today) in Berlin."

Macron stressed that negotiations to end the war would need to involve Ukraine, Europe, the US and Russia seated at the same table.

"Europeans have taken decisions. They have decided to determine their own fate," the French president said. "Europe is not a subject on a menu of discussions, but a series of powers who want to build their own future".

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Macron's message, saying "there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room (and) there's no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room".

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the meeting in Berlin bore "testament" to Russia's failure to sow division among European allies.

The four leaders agreed that the time has come for Europe to engage in face-to-face negotiations with Russia, marking a step that has yet to take place in the negotiation process.

Europe has appointed a joint team of seven representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, Italy, the EU institutions and NATO for the next round of talks.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who flew to Berlin to attend the meeting, also called on Russia to allow European participation.

"We do believe that having Europe at the table will be essential to ending this war in a just and long-term, durable way," Kushner said at the closing press conference.

"And the Russians are willing to trust that instinct on our behalf."

Moscow, though, has not committed to a multilateral format.

Speaking in Shenzhen, Putin said he had suggested "via diplomatic channels that the Europeans come to Moscow to define their positions," and, after that, the Kremlin would "decide on continuing the dialogue with Ukraine".

Putin also said that it "would be strange to discuss Europe's security without Europe itself", referring to the demands that Moscow has tabled to restructure the continent's security architecture, which Macron slammed as "maximalist".

Merz said the debate on European security would happen only after peace has been established in Ukraine. The future security guarantees to the war-weary country will inherently have "repercussions" for the transatlantic alliance, he said.

Among the guarantees in the works is a clause emulating NATO's Article 5 of collective defence should Russia attack Ukraine again. Another guarantee would be a Europe-led peacekeeping force, which Putin says he would not allow in any scenario.

"From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," Kushner said. "And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that."

During the closed-door discussions in Berlin, Trump phoned in from his plane and addressed the room, Kushner confirmed. Media reports suggest that Trump expressed scepticism about Europe's military support for Ukraine.

Leaders seemed unmoved and agreed that assistance will continue unabatedto put Ukraine in a strong position at the negotiating table.

"I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow," Burnham said.

"For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine, and we will not falter. Our support will be unwavering. And that's the biggest weapon we have together."

The US, Chinese and Russian leaders pledged to hold talks on nuclear risk reduction, but made no mention of North Korea in their joint peace declaration.

US President Donald Trump left China on Thursday without meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a get-together he had sought during his visit to Shenzhen for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Trump had repeatedly raised the possibility of meeting Kim during his Asia trip, although a White House official had said no such meeting was planned.

“We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday.

Meanwhile, Kim inspected sites in North Korea’s South Hamgyong province on Tuesday and Wednesday, according to South Korean news agency Newsis.

The two leaders have not met face-to-face since June 2019.

Although the three leaders agreed to pursue dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation, the joint “peace declaration” made no explicit reference to the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan.

However, Chinese state news agency Xinhua later reported that the three leaders had exchanged views on the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, nuclear non-proliferation and the situation in the Middle East.

The summit has fuelled concerns in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan that major powers could make decisions affecting regional security without consulting those directly affected.

South Korea fears being sidelined

Before the three-way meeting, South Korean media compared it to the Yalta Conference in 1945, where leaders of the US, the UK and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war international order.

Seoul has been keen to avoid major powers making decisions on the Korean peninsula without its involvement.

Although the omission of the Korean peninsula from the declaration has somewhat alleviated concerns over a second Yalta, it has raised concerns that denuclearisation is slipping down the major powers’ diplomatic agenda, according to South Korean news outlet Money Today.

Park Won-gon, a professor of North Korean studies at Ewha Womans University, told the outlet that China and Russia may have sided with Pyongyang.

Kim Jae-chun, a professor at Sogang University, said the three powers view North Korea’s nuclear programme very differently.

However, Newsis suggested that the absence of a Trump-Kim meeting for the second consecutive year may ease concerns over potential US recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state.

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung reiterated, during Thursday’s APEC summit, the importance of achieving peace and stability on the Korean peninsula to bring prosperity to the region.

Japan seeks reassurances from Washington

The three-way meeting has raised concerns in Japan, where relations with Beijing are tense.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi exchanged greetings with Xi during APEC, but the two leaders did not meet formally.

A Japanese ruling-party lawmaker said Japan’s exclusion from the three-way meeting could be seen as a diplomatic setback, Fuji TV reported.

However, Takaichi said at a press briefing in Shenzhen that she did not believe Japan’s interests would be undermined by the summit, Japanese broadcaster TBS reported.

Takaichi is also arranging a phone call with Trump to discuss the outcome of his talks with Xi and Putin and reaffirm bilateral cooperation, TV Asahi reported, citing Japanese government sources.

Japanese media also highlighted the three powers’ position on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is currently headed by Japanese judge Tomoko Akane.

The joint declaration called for respect for the immunity of state officials and said that the ICC and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction.

In March 2023, the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.

Taiwan wary of great-power diplomacy

As with South Korea, mentions of "Yalta 2.0" emerged in Taiwanese media in the lead-up to the meeting. Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS highlighted concerns that Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in the negotiations.

The question of Taiwan was raised in the bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump earlier on Thursday.

Tsai Jung-hsiang, a professor of political science at National Chung Cheng University in Taiwan, told the island’s Central News Agency that the US and China have very different views on strategic stability.

While Trump has aimed to avoid conflict over Taiwan during his time in office, Xi wanted the US to recognise Beijing’s position on sovereignty and territorial integrity, Tsai said.

However, he said he did not expect any changes to US policy regarding Taiwan as a result of the meeting.

State-run media in China said the three-way meeting allowed the three major powers to work together to promote international security and stability.

Xi said the meeting was “positive, constructive and fruitful”, as the three nations were committed to “world peace”, Xinhua reported.

Earlier, Xi said the three nations should hold regular high-level meetings and establish mechanisms to prevent and manage crises.

Neither proposal was explicitly included in the four-point peace declaration.

Atacul a fost detectat pe 22 octombrie, iar Comisia Europeană a confirmat joi că a intervenit pentru a limita efectele unei campanii cibernetice în care au fost folosite instrumente de inteligență artificială. Purtătorul de cuvânt al instituției, Thomas Regnier, a declarat că mai multe aplicații au fost dezactivate temporar, ca măsură de protecție, iar cele mai multe au fost între timp repuse în funcțiune.

Potrivit informațiilor publicate de Politico, întreruperile au durat aproximativ 10 zile și au afectat inclusiv sistemele interne de resurse umane, folosite de angajați pentru accesarea fluturașilor de salariu, gestionarea concediilor și pontaj, precum și platforma pentru decontarea cheltuielilor medicale. Au fost afectate și serviciile de traducere. Comisia Europeană are aproximativ 33 de mii de angajați.

Instituția nu a stabilit încă dacă atacatorii au reușit să extragă date personale și nici care este amploarea eventualelor compromiteri. Regnier a precizat că nu există indicii privind o breșă de date care să afecteze personalul Comisiei în ansamblu și că, până în prezent, nu a fost identificată o cerere de răscumpărare.

Potrivit Politico, atacatorii ar fi folosit ARTEX, un instrument bazat pe inteligență artificială, disponibil public, care poate fi utilizat pentru identificarea vulnerabilităților sistemelor informatice. Astfel de instrumente pot automatiza și accelera procesul de descoperire a unor puncte slabe în rețele și aplicații, ceea ce le poate face utile atât pentru specialiștii în securitate, cât și pentru atacatori. ARTEX a fost folosit și în cadrul unui atac dezvăluit de Google, primul în care inteligența artificială a descoperit vulnerabilități informatice și a dezvoltat automat metode de exploatare a acestora, fără intervenția unui operator uman pe parcursul procesului.

Comisia a convocat cel mai înalt organism intern de gestionare a crizelor, Corporate Management Board, pentru a discuta incidentul, iar comisarul european pentru tehnologie, Henna Virkkunen, a prezentat situația și măsurile luate în cadrul reuniunii Colegiului Comisarilor de miercuri.

Incidentul este unul dintre cele mai recente atacuri cibernetice sau perturbări informatice care au afectat instituții și infrastructuri din mai multe țări. În ultimele luni, au fost raportate atacuri asupra unor supermarketuri din Franța, asupra unor sisteme de transport și infrastructuri informatice, precum și întreruperi care au afectat bănci, servicii Microsoft și alte sisteme.

Hungary is under new leadership, and reforms are underway. But can Péter Magyar restore the rule of law and win back the EU's trust?

EU affairs ministers met on Thursday, 19 November, for the EU's annual rule of law dialogue, which examines judicial independence, corruption, media freedom, and institutional checks and balances.

This is a regular review, not a special hearing against Hungary or a vote on sanctions.

However, the timing is significant, as Brussels assesses whether the changes under Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar are delivering lasting results.

"I think we have seen clear efforts to break with the rule of law situation that has existed under Viktor Orbán and that the new government under Magyar has really put an effort into implementing reforms to restore judicial independence," Thu Nguyen, the Acting Co-Director at the Jacques Delors Centre, told Euronews Verify.

Why is the EU still keeping Hungary under scrutiny?

Since taking office in 2026, Magyar's government has moved quickly to reverse some of the policies that put Hungary on a collision course with the EU.

The emergency rule by decree has ended.

The controversial Sovereignty Protection Office, which investigated civil society organisations and media outlets, has been abolished.

Hungary has also joined the European Public Prosecutor's Office and introduced new anti-corruption and judicial reforms.

A European Parliament delegation visiting Hungary in October praised the pace of these changes, describing them as substantial progress.

Despite all that, Hungary is also still subject to a separate EU procedure known as Article 7.

Launched in 2018, it addresses concerns about a serious risk to the EU's founding values, including democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights.

Could the UK rejoin the EU?

Today's episode also focuses on the long-awaited EU-UK summit that will take place this Friday, 20 November.

After a decade of Brexit, London now wants closer ties with Brussels, not a divorce.

And there is public support too: 56% of Britons would now vote to rejoin.

The reset began under Keir Starmer and picked up pace under Andy Burnham, who stirred the Brexit debate but stopped short of committing to rejoining.

Five European leaders have called for closer collaboration in areas, including on energy.

But will the UK be able to re-join under the same conditions as before, including its opt-outs?

"If the UK were to rejoin the EU, it would not be rejoining the EU that it left," said Sébastien Maillard, associate fellow at Chatham House.

"It's much more a geopolitical EU that would be joining, and it has to be ready [...] to accept the idea of European sovereignty. I think if the UK is ready to go fully on the idea that there is a need to side with the EU as a member state, to build sovereign capacities independently from the US or from China, then it can negotiate all kinds of opt-outs."

How long would it take for the UK to rejoin the bloc?

The UK's Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has held off on the possibility that he could ask to rejoin at some stage, while ruling out major changes before the next election.

"This government has been clear that at least until the next election they are still committed to those red lines, so we wouldn't expect to see the UK's relationship change in this parliament with the European Union," said Oliver Nicholls, senior policy manager of Best for Britain

Yet, the first step to rejoin the bloc is getting the conversation started in the UK.

Inside Nasdaq, co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell to celebrate the start of trading; outside, protesters chanted against the flotation and the concentration of tech-sector wealth in a demonstration that saw three people detained by police.

The listing overtook SpaceX’s blockbuster June offering, highlighting relentless investor enthusiasm for AI despite growing talk of overheated technology valuations. Robust demand carried the share price clear of its earlier $70 to $78 guide range. Yet demonstrators warned that ordinary investors could pay the price if the AI surge ends in a financial bust. Jose Gonzalez, among those protesting outside, questioned who would bear the brunt of a market reversal, arguing that wealthy investors enjoy protections unavailable to the public.

The meteoric surge of artificial intelligence is sparking hope and alarm in equal measure. While global spending on AI approaches $850 billion in 2026 and enthusiasts hail a sweeping economic and technological revolution, economists and watchdogs warn of a looming financial bubble, swelling debt and growing inequality, alongside fears that automation will wipe out jobs and funnel vast wealth into the coffers of a few tech titans.

Aboard the Latvian patrol vessel Valpas, Euronews follows maritime operations and visits a Frontex drone base at Tympaki airfield. A search for missing migrants near Chrissi Island highlights the dangers of the crossing, while temporary reception facilities face growing pressure.

While irregular migration is declining along several routes into the European Union, the opposite is happening on Crete. The Greek island, better known for its beaches and tourism industry, is facing a sharp increase in arrivals from North Africa and Asia.

Around 24,000 migrants reached Crete during the first ten months of 2026, compared with approximately 17,000 throughout 2025.

Most boats depart from eastern Libya, crossing hundreds of kilometres of open sea towards Gavdos, a small island south of Crete, or the southern coastline of Crete itself.

Despite increased patrols, surveillance aircraft and sophisticated monitoring technology, the crossings continue.

To understand what is happening on Europe's southern maritime frontier, Euronews joined a patrol of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Frontex, spending time with its crews at sea and visiting the facilities coordinating aerial surveillance.

A search for missing migrants

During our reporting, an incident illustrated the dangers of this increasingly busy migration route.

On the afternoon of November 4, a migrant was discovered alone on Chrissi Island, approximately 15 kilometres off Crete’s southern coast.

He claimed to have travelled with 60 other people, triggering an extensive search and rescue operation.

It is just one of dozens of incidents requiring a response from Greek and European patrol and rescue teams operating off Crete.

Local Coast Guard officials in Heraklion told Euronews that, in just 48 hours, 13 boats carrying approximately 400 migrants had arrived within their area of responsibility.

During the same period, around 20 migrants were also found dead- a stark reminder of the human cost of the increasingly dangerous crossing to Europe's southern shores.

A Latvian ship guarding Europe's borders

Greece hosts Frontex's largest operational presence in the European Union, with the agency supporting Greek authorities across a wide range of activities.

The agency provides technical equipment, surveillance capabilities and support for return operations involving migrants who have no legal right to remain in the EU. All these activities are carried out in cooperation with the Greek authorities, who retain operational command.

In Crete and Gavdos -the small Greek island south of Crete and the southernmost inhabited island in Europe- alone, more than 40 officers, three aircraft, an unmanned aircraft and six patrol vessels have been deployed to support Greek authorities.

Among them is Valpas, a Latvian patrol vessel operating south of Crete for approximately 18 months. A typical patrol aboard Valpas lasts 72 hours. For its 20-member crew, the ship becomes both a workplace and a temporary home.

Leaving their families behind, crew members try to maintain a connection with Latvia, keeping familiar traditions alive even while operating far from home. Captain Ozers, a father of three, speaks to his children every evening.

Captain Ozers told Euronews that rescue operations can be extremely difficult and dangerous, both for the migrants attempting the crossing and for the crews trying to bring them to safety.

He recalled one of the most challenging moments he has faced at sea:

“Sometimes, everyone tries to stand up at once, which can cause the boat to capsize. I experienced this myself during an operation when two people fell overboard. We were fortunate that only two ended up in the water. It was nighttime, but we managed to keep them in sight throughout. We threw them lifebuoys and other flotation devices while we first secured the larger group of passengers on the boat. Once they were safe, we moved away from the boat and manoeuvred closer to the two people in the water.”

Weather conditions make these operations even more challenging. Captain Ozers explained that one of the greatest dangers arises when migrants set off in favourable weather, only to face deteriorating conditions during their journey.

“The most difficult for us is when they start their voyage with the nice weather and then the weather becomes bad. We need to plan how to pick them up and it becomes a little bit dangerous.”

Ioannis Orphanos, Commander of the Hellenic Coast Guard’s 7th Regional Command, which oversees Coast Guard operations across Crete, explained that rescue operations can be particularly challenging.

“Some incidents are extremely difficult, and unfortunately, there are times when lives are lost. We must remember that the area is vast and weather conditions are often adverse. We may be dealing with people who have never experienced the sea before, who are completely unfamiliar with the maritime environment and may not even know how to swim,” he told Euronews.

Eyes in the sky

Frontex's operations also rely on advanced aerial surveillance. From Tympaki airfield in Crete, Frontex operates the Heron 1, a highly advanced long-endurance surveillance drone equipped with sophisticated radar, high-resolution cameras and thermal imaging technology. It can remain airborne for more than 20 hours, monitoring vast stretches of the Libyan Sea both day and night.

Its images are transmitted live to the Hellenic Coast Guard's operations centre in Piraeus and Frontex headquarters in Warsaw, while Greek authorities retain operational command.

Evangelos Diamantis, Head of the Monitoring and Surveillance Sector at the Frontex Operation Centre, explained why early detection is crucial:

“The boats used by smuggling networks are not seaworthy. They often have faulty engines, which means there is no guarantee they will reach their destination — the European shores, in this case Greece. They are always overcrowded, making them highly vulnerable to sinking or accidents, especially when combined with bad weather. So, detecting these boats early increases the chances of rescuing the people on board and bringing them safely to shore.”

Growing tensions on Crete

Yet increased surveillance has not stopped migrants from reaching the island. Newcomers are transferred directly to four tightly controlled temporary accommodation facilities, where they await transportation to mainland Greece.

The continuing arrivals are fuelling increasingly strong opposition among residents and local authorities, who object to migrants remaining in their communities.

Crete is therefore facing pressure on two fronts: managing a growing number of arrivals while dealing with mounting local resistance.

For the European Union, the challenge extends beyond the Greek island.

As migration routes shift and surveillance capabilities expand, a fundamental question remains: how can Frontex become more effective in managing irregular migration while fulfilling its responsibility to protect human lives at sea?

Disruption to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz is driving up costs for households, while the agency says the longer the crisis continues, the harder it will be for global energy markets to recover.

The Middle East conflict has triggered the largest threat to global energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has warned, as disrupted oil supplies push up prices and leave consumers increasingly exposed to the fallout.

The comments come following the US and Israeli bombing of Iran, which began in February.

The IEA said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook report that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world struggles to find new solutions to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

The agency also warned that, just like previous energy shocks, the crisis will certainly leave "lasting marks".

The IEA made the remarks as Gulf countries continue to struggle with exporting oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following the US and Israeli strikes.

Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the Strait – which carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments before the crisis began – supply lines are still severely disrupted.

"The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.

Birol also highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, as well as China buying less from international markets.

"Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply," he wrote.

The report also mentioned that "increasingly it is falling to consumers – and high prices – to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down".

Back in July, Birol said the oil market was benefiting from "several cushioning factors", something that isn’t in place now, meaning the outlook is far bleaker.

No way back?

The IEA's report comes as leaders meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey.

There, governments are under significant pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, as well as deadly floods in Nepal.

The IEA uses three scenarios for its energy outlook. These are a cautious one, which takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario, which looks at "stated" government policies, including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third, which considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050.

Climate scientist Bill Hare, founder of the Climate Analytics think tank, said the world had to commit to the most interventionist scenario outlined by the IEA.

"If we don't get on the net-zero train the IEA has outlined, then we are condemning the world to irreversible and permanent warming of 2.5C or above," he told the AFP.

In this particular report, the IEA also added two scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists.

"While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be," Birol said in a press release, adding that he doesn't “see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, 34% above their $83 IPO price, putting the Claude maker on track for a $2 trillion valuation (€1.8tn) after it raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in the largest initial public offering in history.

Shares in Anthropic, the AI firm behind the Claude models, opened 34% above their IPO price on the Nasdaq on Thursday, at $111.50 against $83, putting it on course for a $2 trillion (€1.8tn) valuation.

It raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in the biggest stock market listing ever, beating SpaceX's record raise back in June.

That fully diluted value, up from $1.5 trillion (€1.36tn) at the IPO price, puts Anthropic roughly level with SpaceX, the world's sixth most valuable listed company.

In a speech at Nasdaq's opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei stated: "I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade."

"We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," Amodei added, as the company remains locked in a dispute with the Trump administration over military uses of its technology.

President Daniela Amodei said Anthropic had been "a safety company since day one" and bore ultimate responsibility for training its AI models to be safe.

Anthropic priced its shares above its initial $70 to $78 range and enlarged the offering to 980 million shares from 825 million. More than half of the roughly 1,200 institutional investors that bid for shares reportedly got none, with allocations heavily favouring US-based investors.

About 15% of the public offering, or roughly $12 billion (€10.9bn) of shares, went to retail investors, according to Bloomberg citing people familiar with the deal.

That is below the 20% maximum set out in the prospectus and SpaceX's roughly 20% retail allocation, but far above the norm.

Investors including Nvidia, Google and AMD are also buying $26 billion (€23.6bn) of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement, taking the total raised to $107.3 billion (€97.7bn).

The Wall Street banks that ran the deal made an estimated $550 million (€501mn) in fees.

What investors are buying

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI researchers and executives, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now its CEO and president respectively.

Its revenue jumped to about $17 billion (€15.4bn) in the third quarter from $1.4 billion (€1.27bn) a year earlier, and the company puts its annualised revenue at about $81 billion (€73.7bn) as of the end of October.

It booked a $104 billion (€94.7bn) net loss in the first nine months of the year, but almost all of it stems from accounting revaluations that disappear once the company lists.

Excluding stock-based pay and donations, its operations made a $2.5 billion (€2.27bn) profit in the third quarter.

It has also committed at least $518 billion (€471bn) to cloud computing and infrastructure suppliers over roughly a decade.

The founders keep 50.1% of the voting power, while a trust appoints four of the seven board members, a set-up a shareholder advocacy group says leaves investors with almost no voice.

Anthropic is also locked in a dispute with the Trump administration, which in February ordered federal agencies to stop using its technology after the company refused to let Claude be used for mass surveillance of Americans or fully autonomous weapons.

Retail investors in nine European countries, including France, Germany and Spain, were able to apply for shares through participating brokers.

Agenția Internațională pentru Energie (AIE) estimează, într-un raport anual, că centrele de date vor consuma de două ori mai multă energie până în 2030 și că trei sferturi din surplus va fi utilizat pentru a susține eforturile de dezvoltare a inteligenței artificiale. Mai exact, în termen de patru ani, centrele de date pentru inteligență artificială vor consuma, anual, încă 350 de terawați-oră de electricitate în fiecare an, adică mai mult decât consumul anual de electricitate al Marii Britanii. 

În aceste condiții, centrele de date ale lumii vor genera cu 70% mai multe emisii de carbon în următorii patru ani. Toate acestea, în condițiile în care SUA și China se orientează către combustibili fosili pentru a-și susține agendele de dezvoltare a inteligenței artificiale, potrivit AIE.

Agenția estimează că până la sfârșitul deceniului, aproximativ jumătate din energia electrică necesară pentru alimentarea centrelor de date din China va proveni din termocentrale pe cărbune. SUA, în schimb, se așteaptă că se vor baza pe gaze pentru a asigura aproximativ 60% din energia electrică necesară centrelor lor de date până în 2030. În luna august a acestui an, existau planuri pentru aproximativ 180 GW de noi centrale electrice pe gaz, a mai precizat AIE. În UE se estimează că, până în 2030, centrele de date se vor baza pe surse regenerabile pentru aproximativ 70% din energia electrică consumată, fiind urmate de energia nucleară, producția pe bază de gaze și o cantitate foarte mică de energie obținută din cărbune.

In a city renowned for its walnut trees, and at a cultural distance that surpasses geography, a group of culture and art lovers chose to begin a new story called the dialogue between the Arab world and France.

Attended by members of Arab communities, city council representatives and members of the Tunisian consul, the cultural association Les Carthagi'Noix came into being, during a celebratory evening last weekend in Grenoble in south-eastern France.

The choice of name was not a minor detail. Les Carthagi'Noix brings together Carthage, with all its historical and cultural symbolism in Tunisia and the eastern Mediterranean, and the French word "Noix", meaning walnut, one of Grenoble's best known specialities.

From its very first letters, the name embodies the association's core idea, bringing two cultures together and creating a shared space where Arab memory meets the city's local identity.

Speaking at the opening, the association's president, Aya Ben Azzouz, explained that the idea stems from a simple desire to build a cultural link between the Arab world and the Grenoble area by honouring the culture and arts of the Arab region and introducing them to the French public, while at the same time building bridges with the local cultural scene.

Ben Azzouz said that the association hopes this exchange will be present in many fields, from culture and art to music, dance and food, as well as workshops and activities that allow the public to discover different aspects of Arab culture and engage with it directly.

From music to memory: a culture presented through living experiences

Les Carthagi'Noix does not want to limit its work to presenting Arab heritage as something belonging to the past, but aims to show it as a living, evolving culture with its own artists, voices and contemporary experiences.

In this context, Middle Eastern music is one of the areas the association plans to work on, through the "Mouzaik" ensemble, along with art workshops and activities focused on cultural exchange, and on highlighting Arab history and heritage.

Among the association's other goals is to shine a light on Arab artists living in Grenoble and give them the opportunity to present their work and experiences, while also showcasing local artists and creating spaces for collaboration between them and their counterparts from the Arab world.

The association hopes its activities and events will go beyond the Arab communities in Grenoble and reach a wider audience beyond the city.

The association's executive board consists of Aya Ben Azzouz as president, Taieb El Faleh as vice-president, Jihan Al Jaridi as secretary-general, and Adam Abdelhadi as treasurer, while music teacher Abdelaziz Dhib serves as the association's honorary president.

The opening evening included speeches by some members of the executive board, along with artistic and musical segments, during which the "Mouzaik" ensemble performed a selection of Eastern pieces, while the "Mery Muse" band provided the evening's entertainment.

From the outset, Les Carthagi'Noix has set itself a clear target that goes beyond organising one-off events, aiming to build an ongoing presence for Arab culture in Grenoble, engage with local cultural institutions and actors, and create opportunities for meetings between artists and audiences from different backgrounds.

In a city that is used to being a meeting point for many cultures, the association is trying to add a new space to this landscape, one that does not stop at invoking Carthage or celebrating Arab heritage, but explores what can emerge from their encounter with Grenoble.

UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk warned that while AI might sound something futuristic, underneath it is based on an age-old narrative of power.

Artificial intelligence is being governed in an almost mediaeval fashion, the UN rights chief warned Thursday, with power concentrated in the hands of a few tech barons.

Speaking at the RightsX summit in Geneva, UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk said that while the story of AI sounded futuristic, underneath it was an age-old narrative of power.

"A handful of men still control much of the world's AI computing power, data and infrastructure. And we still have no common rules to pace or steer AI development," he said.

Turk said there was a glaring democratic deficit when five technology companies owned more than 70% of global AI computing capacity.

"We have the technology of the future governed in an almost mediaeval way: by a select few, with virtually no checks, no balances, no participation, and no accountability," he said.

"History has taught us: with this kind of power, the rights and freedoms of ordinary people are the first to suffer."

Reiterating his call for rights-centred AI regulation, the UN high commissioner for human rights said the technology was increasingly controlling people's lives.

And this, he warned, was often happening without their knowledge, and could distort public debate in "subtle, insidious ways".

Meanwhile biased algorithms could reproduce injustice on an industrial scale, he cautioned.

'Civilisational collapse'

"Our transport, food and healthcare are increasingly digitised. We may not be far from the day when AI can cut off the critical infrastructure of entire communities or countries, either on its own or in the wrong hands," Turk warned.

"When people discuss the chances of civilisational collapse because of AI, we need to ask: who decides what chances we take?"

He voiced optimism that people would ultimately challenge unchecked power, with the democratic deficit turning into a deficit of trust.

He cited young people already stepping offline to regain greater control of their lives.

Turk said AI's benefits should be shared equitably, which would require goodwill from technology companies, but also regulation and accountability.

He said he had written to frontier AI companies urging them to introduce effective safeguards "before it is too late".

Turk noted that a bottle of milk could not make it to a shop without layers of testing, rules and regulations.

So for AI, "it's a no-brainer that you need some form of regulation", given its potential for harm, Turk said.

As for how models are trained, he suggested giving the Universal Declaration of Human Rights "as the task to AI".

EU ambassadors broadly backed a 10-year probation period for newcomers, with voting rights open to suspension for Orbán-style breaches, as a basis for Montenegro’s treaty.

EU countries have taken the first step towards establishing a 10-year probation period for new members, during which newcomers, starting with Montenegro, could have their voting rights suspended for serious rule-of-law breaches or obstructing EU decisions.

The European Commission unveiled the proposal last month to avoid a repeat of the experience with Hungary under Viktor Orbán, whose government violated the bloc’s basic values and repeatedly wielded its veto to block decisions requiring unanimity.

The Commission initially proposed a 15-year probation period. However, several countries, notably Italy and other members of the Friends of the Western Balkans group, which champions the region's accession, argued that such a long period could hardly be considered temporary.

Ireland, which chairs talks among member states as holder of the rotating EU Council presidency, proposed shortening the period to 10 years, with a possible five-year extension. The proposal received broad support from EU ambassadors on Wednesday.

According to an EU diplomat with direct knowledge of the discussions, ambassadors showed far greater willingness to compromise than the officials who had spent weeks negotiating the details.

The more contentious question is what would trigger a suspension of voting rights. Montenegro, the country closest to joining the bloc, has warned that any decision must be based on objective criteria and systematic breaches of EU values and rules.

Several member states sympathetic to the candidate countries object to including breaches of “sincere cooperation”, the EU treaty principle requiring members to work together in good faith and refrain from jeopardising the bloc’s objectives. They argue that such breaches are difficult to assess objectively.

These countries also oppose suspending new members’ voting rights altogether, fearing the mechanism could be used to force newcomers to abandon positions close to their national interest, creating a de facto second tier of EU members.

Ireland also proposed changing how the safeguard is triggered, with decisions taken by qualified majority, meaning a majority of countries representing at least 65% of the EU’s population. Here, too, member states did not object strongly.

Discussions will now shift from the general rules for future members to how they would apply to Montenegro. Ireland’s proposal will form the basis of the safeguards in Montenegro’s accession treaty, which the Commission aims to have signed by June 2027.

Officials are expected to hold their first technical discussions on a draft of the relevant section of the treaty, Chapter 35, early next week. Podgorica, which cannot negotiate this part of the treaty, has been lobbying member states in the meantime.

What remains unclear is whether the safeguards will be tailored to Montenegro or establish a precedent for all future EU members.

“Carving out single-sector export limits cannot substitute for both, faster regulatory simplification and comprehensive defence of Europe’s industrial baseline against systematic market disruption,” reads the letter, initiated by Slovak MEP Miriam Lexmann (EPP).

The EU faces a trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, while a surge in low-cost Chinese imports is widely seen as a threat to thousands of jobs across European industries.

EU countries gave the Commission a mandate in June to negotiate with Beijing to rebalance trade relations while developing new trade defence tools. In October, France and Germany called for a new instrument that would restrict market access for foreign competitors causing serious market disruption.

In the letter sent to the Commission president, MEPs from the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the largest political group in Parliament, the liberal Renew group, the Socialists and Democrats (S&D), the Greens and the Eurosceptic European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) call for “horizontal” quotas and tariffs to address Chinese overcapacities.

The MEPs also highlight “weak” customs enforcement, which enables tax evasion and breaches of safety rules, and warn that lengthy EU investigations risk leaving European companies facing closure before protective measures are introduced.

“The Commission must now implement a systematic approach,” the letter adds, including regulatory simplification to “ease regulatory burden” on EU companies and the deployment of “horizon-wide” trade defence instruments. The MEPs also call for “strict local supply chain content rules” and the “harmonisation” of EU customs controls.

The letter comes as Šefčovič prepares for talks with his Chinese counterpart, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, in January and March next year.

The Commission is also expected to unveil the new trade defence instrument sought by Paris and Berlin before the end of the year.

Most small business owners don’t have the luxury of delegating. In a survey of 501 French business leaders by OpinionWay for Alibaba.com, 78% said everything rested on their shoulders, while six in ten spent too much time on repetitive tasks.¹

Taking a business into a new country adds more work, whether it’s finding suppliers or understanding the differences in regulations. For an owner already doing most of the heavy lifting, expanding abroad can feel daunting.

“For SMEs, complexity is often one of the biggest challenges of doing business, particularly when it comes to sourcing, supplier assessment and operating internationally,” explains Patrick Sostmann, General Manager Europe at Alibaba.com.

Despite these challenges, the appetite for international trade is growing among European SMEs. Alibaba.com, the business-to-business marketplace connecting buyers and suppliers in more than 200 countries and regions, says the number of products listed by European sellers has surged by 78% to 1.28 million. European order numbers have grown by 70% over the past three years.

The challenge for smaller firms is making the most of that growth without taking on more work. Alibaba.com believes AI can help through Accio, its agentic AI platform built specifically for the needs and budgets of small businesses. Accio’s AI agents for e-commerce are specifically designed to help founders research markets, find products, assess suppliers and manage sourcing.

Growing confidence in AI

Research by the Small Business Institute and Alibaba.com found that 70% of UK small business owners feel confident using generative AI, yet fewer than half (48%) use it regularly. Of those who do, 74% use it for content and marketing, while just 5% apply it to supply chain management. Familiarity has grown faster than the hours saved, highlighting the AI productivity gap.

68% want to learn more about AI agents, while half believe the technology could give them more time to find new customers.

Priorities vary across Europe. In Italy, a Censuswide survey for Alibaba.com found that 23% of SME decision-makers saw the greatest potential for AI in customs procedures and import documentation, followed by comparing suppliers and prices (22%).² In Germany, 32% of respondents to a YouGov study for Alibaba.com and the e-commerce association bevh (Bundesverband E-Commerce und Versandhandel Deutschland) identified administrative overload as a challenge.³

AI: From Ask to Task

While a chatbot can answer a question, an agentic AI platform, such as Accio, can take on a multi-step task. It can gather market data, compare suppliers and pull quotes together before an owner signs off on a purchase.

An effective AI agent needs three things: a model to provide the intelligence, a harness, which is the set of tools it uses to carry out tasks, and context, which is the business knowledge behind its decisions. Alibaba refers to this as Model × Harness × Context.

Capable and affordable

Powerful technology is of little use to a small business if it costs too much. As Kuo Zhang, President of Alibaba.com, puts it, “for small businesses, unaffordable AI is useless.”

Accio breaks larger requests into smaller steps and identifies the most efficient way to handle each one, using lighter models for routine work and more powerful ones when a task needs deeper analysis. It can also reuse information and coordinate agents to avoid duplicating work. By matching resources to the complexity of each task, it can keep costs down.

In Alibaba.com’s benchmark of 107 e-commerce tasks, the company reports an estimated total cost of $3.69 for the full task set. This was more than 50% lower than general-purpose agents in the comparison, with comparable quality. The benchmark, Commerce Agent Bench, is publicly available for others to examine.

Alibaba.com expects the next step in business-to-business trade to be agent-to-agent (A2A) transactions, with digital agents handling more of the buying and selling.

Seeing it work

Alibaba.com’s flagship event CoCreate Europe, a two-day event opening in London on 19 November, demonstrates in practice how access to AI-powered tools and global sourcing opportunities can help businesses turn promising product ideas into commercially viable ventures. For the first time this year, Alibaba.com is introducing the ‘One Person Company (‘OPC’) Market which brings together 30 founder-led European brands to show what it takes to turn an idea into a business. Across beauty, fashion, homeware, food and outdoor products, visitors can meet the people behind the brands, experience their products and discover how they were developed.

Owners will still need to weigh up risks and make the big decisions. But if AI agents can take some research and routine work off their hands, growing internationally may become more manageable.

Perhaps the next survey will find fewer business owners feeling that everything rests on them.

Sickness absence costs the EU up to €810 billion every year, highlighting the need for better prevention and earlier treatment to reduce its economic impact, a new report has found.

The average European misses nearly three weeks of work each year due to ill health, a new report has found.

This accounts for around 6% of potential working time in the European Union, representing about €540 billion in lost labour costs each year, according to the report by the Environment and Public Health Institute. That is equivalent to 2.9% of the EU’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025.

However, this figure captures only part of the economic impact of ill health, which includes everything from viral infections to mental health issues or cancer. The calculation covers only sickness-related absence among people who are still classified as full-time employees and does not take into account the full economic cost of long-term ill health, the report noted.

A person who needs to reduce their working hours or leaves the labour market due to illness is no longer recorded as a sickness absence.

Beyond the direct loss of working time, illness also carries wider economic consequences.

When people are unable to work because of illness, economic output also declines, while employers and colleagues have to manage the consequences of their absence, such as hiring a replacement or asking other employees to work overtime.

Longer periods of sickness absence can also lead people to leave the labour market altogether, reducing tax revenues and increasing spending on social insurance, the report noted.

Taking these direct and indirect costs into account, the report calculated an additional cost of around €135 billion to €270 billion per year, bringing the total annual cost to €675 billion to €810 billion.

How much sick leave do people take across Europe?

While economic loss for sick absences is a Europe-wide issue, there is a “dramatic difference across Europe”, Adrian Mehic, author of the report, said while presenting the report at the European Parliament in Brussels. 

According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Slovenia had the longest average sick leave in 2025, with just over five weeks per employee, followed by around five weeks in Finland and Spain.

France, Sweden and Germany are slightly above three weeks, while in Italy and Greece, full-time employees average less than one week of sickness absence.

However, these figures do not necessarily reflect differences in population health, the report warned.

A country recording fewer sickness absences may have a healthier population, but it can also reflect low compensation, weak employment protections or people going to work despite being ill.

How can the economic burden be reduced?

Reasons for sick absences range from poor mental health and musculoskeletal diseases to accidents and chronic illnesses.

But a significant proportion of these absences could potentially be prevented or shortened. Many are linked to conditions for which preventive measures, early treatment and rehabilitation can potentially reduce both the risk and duration of the absences, the report noted.

Preventive measures include better workplace ergonomics, earlier treatment for mental health concerns, faster access to primary care, physiotherapy, mental health and earlier detection of risks, Mehic said.

“Prevention itself is also costly, so not all of these things are free, but properly implemented, the benefits would be bigger than the costs,” he added.

Aleksandar Čupić's appointment marks a historic breakthrough for the grassroots movement, which ended 14 years of rule by Aleksandar Vučić's party after campaigning against corruption.

Serbia's student-led opposition has taken a major step towards forming a government and ending the era of Aleksandar Vučić, appointing a university lecturer as parliament speaker after its election victory last month.

Aleksandar Čupić, a lecturer, doctor of science and assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, won 140 votes in the 250-member assembly, while the Serbian Progressive Party candidate won just 97.

The new generation of student-backed lawmakers are mostly teachers, professors and experts with established careers but little or no political experience.

It’s the first time in Serbia’s history that a grassroots protest movement has won the majority needed to form a government.

“I have been given a huge honour, obligation and responsibility,” Čupić said after his election. He promised to restore Parliament's dignity and “dialogue and tolerance” among the lawmakers.

“I pledge to be strict and just in this position, as I always have been in life,” he added.

Last month’s parliamentary election marked a significant shift for Serbia. Over the preceding 14 years, Vučić’s party had been in charge at all levels of power and was accused of stifling democratic freedoms while allowing crime and corruption to flourish.

Vučić has denied all of the accusations.

The students' election victory came after they led anti-corruption protests for two years following a canopy collapse at a train station in northern Serbia that killed 16 people in November 2024. Many involved in the demonstrations blamed the disaster on rampant corruption in construction projects.

Čupić's election as speaker came after more than two days of heated debate, which was dominated by Vučić's accusations that his opponents were attacking and pressuring him and his party. That’s despite the fact that they still control the government administration and other state institutions.

According to Serbia’s laws, a new government must be voted into office within 90 days after the new Parliament's first session. In his role as speaker, Čupić will also serve as Serbia's acting president. He’s expected to schedule an early presidential election in due course, which must be held by the end of the year.

Vučić has accused the students of “revolutionary terror”, following a surge in post-election arrests which included officials, police officers and a private bank owner who allegedly attempted to siphon off money.

Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, but its bid stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and close ties with Russia.

Many people with iron deficiency aren’t diagnosed right away.

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency, affecting over a billion people worldwide — yet many people do not realise they aren’t getting enough iron.

Iron, which is found in red meat, beans, dried fruit and other foods, is an essential mineral that plays a major role in the body. It helps make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, and myoglobin, which supplies oxygen to the muscles. Iron is also needed for energy production, immune function, growth and brain development.

When someone doesn’t get or retain enough iron, they may experience fatigue or difficulty concentrating — or no symptoms at all. As the body’s iron stores run out, iron deficiency can progress to iron deficiency anaemia, which makes it harder for blood to transport oxygen in the body and can lead to serious complications.

“People rarely die of iron deficiency, but it has a very big effect globally,” Hal Drakesmith, a professor of iron biology at the University of Oxford, told Euronews. “If you don't have enough iron, you don't have enough energy.”

Some people are at higher risk of iron deficiency, including teen girls and women with heavy periods. Pregnant women and their foetuses, infants and children all need extra iron for growth and development, which diet alone can’t always provide.

Older people can become iron deficient due to intestinal bleeding or chronic health problems. A 2022 study found that iron deficiency is fairly common among relatively healthy older adults in Europe. Those aged 80 or older and living in Austria and Portugal were at the highest risk.

Diets low in red meat or other iron-rich foods may also contribute to iron deficiency. Frequent blood donors can become iron deficient, though they are usually tested before they give blood, Drakesmith said.

“It is enormously common,” Drakesmith said.

Even so, many people with iron deficiency aren’t diagnosed right away. Common symptoms are vague and not specific to iron deficiency, and it takes time to develop because people don’t lose all of their iron at once, Drakesmith said.

Iron and ferritin, a protein that stores iron, have become hot topics in wellness circles. A viral claim that people with low iron have “ferritin face” — visible signs such as pale skin and thinning hair — is “not clinically useful,” Drakesmith said. But if the trend raises awareness about iron deficiency and prompts people with symptoms to seek testing, he’s all for it.

Routine screening for iron deficiency is rare, even among higher-risk groups, said Elaine McCarthy, a senior lecturer in nutrition at University College Cork in Ireland. For example, while blood checks are standard in pregnancy, they typically measure haemoglobin.

“This is a problem as haemoglobin is a very late-stage indicator of changes in iron status, meaning we miss those individuals in the earliest stage of the deficiency and miss the opportunity to prevent it worsening,” McCarthy told Euronews.

She advocates for testing both haemoglobin and ferritin, which serves as “a marker of the earliest changes in iron status.”

In September, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) issued new clinical guidance for diagnosing iron deficiency. It suggests that adults, pregnant women and those with periods be diagnosed if their serum ferritin is 30 micrograms per litre or lower, instead of 15 µg/L. That’s in line with recommendations from the European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation.

However, identifying the right ferritin threshold has not been settled globally, Drakesmith said.

“Where you set that ferritin threshold basically will determine the prevalence” of iron deficiency, Drakesmith said. “I think they're erring on the side of making sure they don't miss the diagnosis, which is perfectly sensible. But at the same time, you might end up including people who probably aren't that iron deficient.”

Relying only on ferritin levels also won’t catch everyone with an iron deficiency. People with inflammatory conditions, such as chronic kidney disease, can have normal or even high ferritin levels but still be low in iron. Inflammation in the body can cause ferritin levels to rise even when iron stores are low.

People with inflammatory conditions may have a serum ferritin of up to 100 µg/L and still be iron deficient, according to the European recommendations.

Iron deficiency can often be fixed with supplements, as long as its underlying cause is identified and addressed. But iron supplements can cause side effects such as constipation and stomach pain, which can make people reluctant to stick with them, Drakesmith said.

Too much iron can also be a problem, McCarthy said. Very high doses can be fatal, especially for children.

“You shouldn’t take an iron supplement unless you have been diagnosed with iron deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia,” McCarthy said. “High-dose iron supplements can be dangerous if your body doesn’t actually need the iron.”

European champions Italy and four European debutants are among the 48 teams taking part, while last year’s finalists Portugal and Austria are absent. Qatar is hosting the second of five consecutive editions from 2025 to 2029. The final is on 13 December.

The FIFA Under-17 World Cup got under way in Qatar on Thursday, with 48 teams taking part, including 11 from Europe.

Eight matches were on the opening-day programme at Doha’s Aspire Zone, including France against Haiti, Greece against Egypt and hosts Qatar against Panama.

The 104-match tournament ends with the final at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium on 13 December.

Greece, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia are making their first appearances at the U-17 World Cup. For Montenegro, it also marks the country’s first appearance at any FIFA World Cup.

Italy enter as European champions after beating Belgium on penalties in June’s final, while France are seeking their first U-17 world title since 2001.

Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, Ireland and Spain complete Europe’s line-up.

Defending champions Portugal and last year’s runners-up Austria are both absent after failing to qualify.

The Dominican Republic replaced the US, which withdrew over security concerns. FIFA said the US decision was linked to an existing travel advisory for Qatar and that its own security assessment remained unchanged.

Qatar is hosting the second of five consecutive editions, from 2025 to 2029. The tournament expanded from 24 to 48 teams last year.

All matches except the final will be played across eight pitches at Aspire Zone.

The teams are divided into 12 groups of four. The top two in each group and the eight best third-placed sides will advance to the round of 32. The group stage ends on 27 November, with the knockout rounds beginning on 30 November.

Past participants include Neymar, Phil Foden and Victor Osimhen.

Jeremy Lewin, șeful departamentului de planificare din cadrul Departamentului de Stat, i-a transmis secretarului de Externe al Guyanei, Robert Persaud, în timpul unei întâlniri desfășurate în septembrie la Washington, că poate ajuta la medierea unor discuții teritoriale cu Delcy Rodríguez (care acționa în calitate de președinte al Venezuelei), a precizat una dintre surse pentru Reuters.

Alte două surse au afirmat că Lewin – un oficial important numit de Administrația Trump, care a părăsit Departamentul de Stat la sfârșitul lunii octombrie – a avansat ideea ca Venezuela să preia controlul parțial asupra regiunii Essequibo, care cuprinde două treimi din teritoriul Guyanei. Remarca i-a șocat pe oficialii micii națiuni producătoare de petrol, care au reiterat că statutul regiunii Essequibo nu este negociabil, au precizat sursele.

Într-un interviu acordat agenției Reuters, Lewin a declarat că a purtat discuții ”preliminare” cu reprezentanții Guyanei și ai Venezuelei cu privire la disputa teritorială dintre cele două națiuni. Lewin a explicat că aceste discuții au avut loc după ce, în luna mai, Rodríguez i-a trimis o scrisoare președintelui Donald Trump, solicitând medierea SUA, pentru a facilita negocieri directe cu Guyana privind statutul teritoriului respectiv.

Lewin a adăugat că Rodríguez a abordat subiectul și direct cu el, în timpul unei întâlniri care a avut loc la Caracas, în luna iulie. Toate aceste conversații au fost coordonate și autorizate în totalitate de către Casa Albă, a subliniat Lewin.

Acest episod scoate în evidență legăturile tot mai strânse dintre Administrația Trump și guvernul condus de Rodríguez, notează Reuters. În urma unei operațiuni americane care a dus la capturarea fostului președinte Nicolás Maduro la începutul acestui an, guvernul de la Caracas a deschis larg ușa unei implicări mai accentuate a SUA în afacerile interne ale țării.

Un oficial al Departamentului de Stat a transmis, la solicitarea Reuters, că instituția primește zilnic ”diverse idei și opțiuni de politică din partea unor actori externi”, însă a subliniat că poziția SUA cu privire la granița dintre Venezuela și Guyana a rămas neschimbată.

Venezuela revendică de mult timp regiunea Essequibo – o zonă din Guyana bogată în aur, diamante și bauxită –, însă SUA și toate celelalte țări din lume recunosc acest teritoriu ca aparținând Guyanei.

Data centres could use roughly 1,000 terawatt-hours of power annually by 2030 under the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Stated Policies Scenario.

The amount of electricity used by data centres could double by 2030, reaching up to 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year, straining energy grids and driving carbon emissions up 70%, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

In the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario report, the organisation warns that the rise in electricity demand could stretch power grids and even delay new projects.

The report cited data centre projects in Finland, the United Kingdom, and the United States in states such as Texas and Virginia.

It estimates that electricity would account for nearly 30% of global final energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% in the IEA’s main scenarios.

Peak electricity demand is projected to rise 40% to 50% by 2035, according to the IEA. In the report, grids should be expanded by 26 million kilometres of new lines by 2035, while about 16 million kilometres of existing lines need to be replaced or refurbished.

The IEA also warned that the supplies of copper, transformers and cables needed for data centres are already lacking and grid spending is projected to rise 75% over the next decade.

The report comes as backlash grows against data centres in the US and Europe due to their impact on local communities' public infrastructure, land, water and energy use.
